data.title: Musk says he was behind Starlink disruptions, claiming Ukraine service violations
data.description:
Musk says he was behind Starlink speed restriction after service in Ukraine is restored

SUSIE BLANN and ELISE MORTON
Updated Sat, October 24, 2026 at 10:45 AM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Elon Musk said on Saturday that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, disrupting operations that the country relies on to defend itself against Russia.

Musk's admission on social media came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite links has been restored to the speeds it had before restrictions that disrupted front-line operations for more than a week.

Questions have persisted since last week about who ordered the interruptions to the Musk-made satellite internet system that Kyiv has relied on for years to counter Moscow's attacks.

Advertisement

"The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that restoration began overnight and were sufficient by Saturday morning, improving front-line logistics and defense against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.

Musk admits he was behind Starlink's speed restriction

After Ukraine said the services had been restored, Elon Musk spoke out on the speed restrictions that began last week. In a post Saturday on X, Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX throttled the Starlink satellite internet service.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote. "Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

But he maintained that the U.S. government controlled whatever changes happened with Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communication. He also defended the role of SpaceX in bolstering Ukraine's defenses since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Restrictions imposed last week on Starshield alarmed the country's military and government officials, with commanders reporting lost drones and disrupted missions.

The restoration follows a new U.S. diplomatic push to end the war. Russia agreed Wednesday to resume three-way negotiations with Washington and Kyiv next month. On Friday, Kyiv and Moscow also agreed to a localized ceasefire brokered by first lady Melania Trump around Oleshky, a war-ravaged, Russian-occupied town in Ukraine's southern Kherson region.

Restriction led to tensions between Ukraine and the US

The episode added to tensions between Kyiv and Washington, a relationship already strained by President Donald Trump's reported deal with Moscow on Russian diesel imports, which Ukraine viewed as a betrayal.

Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara credited "direct dialogue" and Zelenskyy's diplomacy with Washington, adding that the outcome mattered most "for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications."

Trump has maintained that he didn't make the call, while also saying Musk should not be blamed. Vice President JD Vance has hinted at White House coordination with Musk, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have denied any administration involvement.

Russia and Ukraine have continued to target each other

Meanwhile, a man was killed and two others wounded in a missile attack on the city of Lozova in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, local officials said Saturday.

Moscow-installed authorities in cities across Russia-occupied Crimea reported power blackouts Saturday following overnight Ukrainian attacks.

Ukraine's General Staff said Saturday that its forces hit a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti, which produces materials used in rocket fuel. Tolyatti Mayor Ilya Sukhikh said the overnight attack damaged industrial facilities in the city.

Ukrainian forces also hit an electronics plant in the city of Oryol, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed Saturday. Local officials in Oryol said Saturday that three people were killed in Friday's attack. The General Staff said the plant makes components for the cruise and ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities.

Ukrainian drones also reached Russia's Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles) from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Gov. Vitaly Khotsenko said drones "reached a northern industrial hub."

Online retailer Ozon said Saturday that its logistics center in Omsk has been attacked by a drone, but there were no casualties. Ozon is a competitor to Wildberries, whose facilities Ukraine has also targeted.

___

Morton reported from London.

___

Follow the AP's coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

data.title: DOJ wants California to set aside 20,000 voters' ballots. The state is refusing.
data.description:
DOJ tells California counties to set aside ballots from suspected noncitizens. Here’s what to know.

The Justice Department says more than 20,000 likely noncitizens were mailed ballots. California officials say the federal data is unreliable and the demand comes too late.

Jack Brewster
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 6:10 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The Justice Department is pressing California election officials to set aside mail-in ballots from people it believes are noncitizens. It is warning that officials who count those ballots could face criminal charges.

Federal prosecutors sent letters Friday to county election offices across the state, giving them 48 hours to work with federal agencies to determine who on a government list is a citizen. NBC News reported that the letters went to 57 of California's 58 counties. Los Angeles County received a similar letter last week.

The secretary of state and Los Angeles County have refused the demand, and other counties are weighing their response. The fight is now before a federal appeals court, 10 days before Election Day.

Advertisement

Here's what to know.

What is the Justice Department asking for?

The department wants counties to "segregate — not cancel" the mail-in ballots of people on its list until their citizenship can be confirmed, according to a letter to San Bernardino County obtained by NBC News. That county's list included 1,133 names.

It also asked counties to send identifying information about the voters on the list, including Social Security numbers and copies of their registrations, the AP reported.

"Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, who signed the letters.

Why does the administration say it's necessary?

The Department of Homeland Security compared California's voter registration files with federal immigration records. It flagged more than 20,000 people it says are "likely" noncitizens who are registered to vote, according to a Justice Department release. Under California law, every registered voter is mailed a ballot.

Only U.S. citizens may vote in federal and state elections. "Even one noncitizen vote cancels out the ballot of an American citizen," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in the release.

Essayli says the request is limited. "We're not asking California to take any drastic steps other than to sequester the ballots from the suspected noncitizens," he told Fox News.

Why is California refusing?

State officials say the federal data hasn't been verified, and that acting on it could keep eligible citizens from voting. In court filings, lawyers for the state argued that counties lack both the authority and the federal records needed to check citizenship. They also said the demand could delay certification of the results.

Some ballots can't be pulled back at all. Once a mail-in ballot's signature is verified, it is separated from its envelope and counted with the others. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed, according to court filings.

Dean Logan, the county's top election official, said the letters carry "a posture of intimidation and threats" just before the election, CNN reported. Sen. Alex Padilla, a Democrat of California, said the administration "has not provided any evidence for their claims of massive voter fraud."

How common is noncitizen voting?

Cases do happen, but reviews have found very few. In 2024, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, a Republican, audited the state's voter rolls and found 20 noncitizens among about 8.2 million registered voters.

Federal claims have not always held up. In August, DHS told Nevada officials it had flagged about 15,900 possible noncitizen registrants. It later said that number was preliminary and that it had confirmed only 185 through manual review, CNN reported. In September, Nevada officials said their own review found that all 185 were U.S. citizens. DHS disputes that finding.

What does this mean for California voters?

For now, nothing has changed. No court has ordered California to set aside any ballots, and counties are still processing the ballots voters return. Voters can check the status of their ballot through the secretary of state's ballot tracking tool.

What happens next?

The Justice Department sued California and Los Angeles County on Oct. 15 to block the ballots from being counted. U.S. District Judge David Carter scheduled a hearing for Tuesday. The department asked the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to step in sooner, and the appeals court ordered California to respond by noon Saturday.

data.title: Republican billionaire Rick Jackson walks a Trump tightrope in Georgia governor bid
data.description:
Republican billionaire Rick Jackson is walking a Trump tightrope in his quest to lead Georgia

BILL BARROW
Updated Sat, October 24, 2026 at 4:38 PM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Trump

1 of 3
Georgia gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson speaks before President Donald Trump arrives at a campaign rally at Dalton Municipal Airport, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026, in Dalton Ga. (AP Photo/Mike Stewart) (AP Photo/Mike Stewart)

ATLANTA (AP) — He's hardly the first billionaire to promise working-class voters he'll fight for them in public office. Rick Jackson, the Republican candidate for Georgia governor, has even compared himself to the real estate mogul who reached the Oval Office.

But Jackson's path differs from Donald Trump's, and the 72-year-old healthcare magnate and investor brings a vastly different persona to his first campaign. Unlike Trump, who was born to wealth, Jackson spent his early years bouncing through foster homes before launching his first company as a young man.

Now, he wants to leverage both his similarities and contrasts with the president, a challenge he's tackling with buckets of his own campaign cash and a personal story that anchors his appeal to voters.

Advertisement

"I have lived in poverty," Jackson says. "When you have not eaten, you never forget that, and you don't forget the people that are struggling."

Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor, disputes Jackson's altruistic pitch, setting up the Nov. 3 election as a test of whether an alternate, softer version of conservative billionaire politics can complement or even counter Trump's pugilistic populism in a key swing state.

Jackson planned to join Trump at a rally Saturday in Perry, in what would be his second appearance with the president in the closing stretch of the campaign.

'From foster care to billionaire'

"My father left me at nine months old. My mother was a sixth-grade educated waitress with a severe alcohol problem," Jackson said in the only debate of their general election campaign. "I had seven stepfathers before I was 12. I lived in the projects, went to 13 different schools, and lived in five different foster homes."

He left college to start a business at 21. That led to Jackson Healthcare, a behemoth company that provides contract nurses and other workers to hospitals and health systems, including public entities that have helped fuel Jackson's fortunes with taxpayer money.

At events with supporters, Jackson gets more personal.

"I have, because of my background, severe abandonment issues," he told hundreds of voters in Cleveland, a conservative enclave in the north Georgia mountains. He turns that acknowledgment into a promise: "Let me tell you one thing: I will never abandon you."

Rags-to-riches themes are not uncommon in politics, and it's yielded Jackson's campaign motto: "From foster care to billionaire." But the scale is eye-popping, illuminated by the nearly $200 million Jackson has spent personally on the campaign. That puts him among the largest self-funding candidates in the history of American elections.

But on that score, too, Jackson tries to soften the caricature of the billionaire executive.

"It's not my money," he said in a northern suburb of Atlanta. Jackson calls his fortune "God's money" and says that "my job is to have kingdom impact" with it.

"The reason I have spent so much money to do this," he said, is to "help 11 million Georgians, to keep them from struggling."

A range of images over a long campaign

Jackson launched his bid as a relative unknown, though Capitol insiders knew him because of Jackson Healthcare, its lucrative state contracts and his lobbying interest in healthcare, business and tax policy.

The Republican primary field featured a trio of statewide elected officials, including Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, who won Trump's endorsement in August 2025, before Jackson got in.

During the primary, Jackson embraced the president even though he wasn't Trump's choice. Jackson sometimes promised to "be like Trump, but with Southern tone." He pledged to "deliver for Georgia the same type of business solutions that President Trump is bringing to our country."

Largely aligning himself with Trump on immigration, Jackson promised to make Georgia a national leader in deportations.

"I don't care if you're Muslim or Mongolian, you don't have the right to force your culture on our country," he said in one ad. "Criminal illegals" who "commit sick, violent crimes" would "end up deported or departed," he promised.

Soon after defeating Jones in a runoff, Jackson shelved the immigration ad, but not before using it as part of a spot featuring his grandchildren. "Granddad, why do you look so mean in these ads?" one asks after watching the "deported or departed" clip on her phone. The children and teenagers then tell their grandfather how he can "look cool" with a pickup truck, a dog and a hipper wardrobe.

"Let's make Georgia better together," the redressed Jackson concludes.

He has since circulated an ad with several young adults who benefited from the millions he spent helping foster children who age out of the Georgia system when they turn 18. "I am so proud of you," he tells them as he chokes up.

On policy, Republican fare and centrist appeals

As he softens his image, Jackson maintains traditional Republican positions, pledging to cut taxes, regulation and what he describes as waste. If he cannot halve the state income tax in four years, he promises not to seek a second term. He wants a balanced budget and full audits of state spending, without saying state law requires a balanced budget and audits of state agencies have long been standard practice.

He says he will expand healthcare without expanding Medicaid under the 2010 Affordable Care Act. Instead, he argues he can fund broader coverage through partnerships with private insurers. That would require Washington to grant permission and commit a level of financial support that no state has gotten without expanding the traditional Medicaid program.

Jackson says he can do all of that while increasing spending on teacher salaries and vocational education.

At the same time, he has toned down his Trump adulation, reflecting Georgia's general election math and voters' frustrations with the Iran war and inflation.

In July, Jackson stood with Trump in Marietta and expressed his hope to "be this guy's favorite governor." When Trump returned to Dalton on Oct. 16, Jackson did not mention Trump at all in his own speech. Later, when the president called him on stage, Jackson praised Trump — for advocating for foster children. When Trump announced that he would be back to Georgia on Saturday, Jackson's campaign initially planned its own event in metro Atlanta before changing it up so Jackson would again be with the president.

Bottoms disputes Jackson's everyman appeal

Bottoms says Jackson is "trying to buy this election" so he can be a Trump stooge. And Democrats have seized on the way that Jackson has talked about the economy.

Discussing trade schools, Jackson said on the debate stage that "my plumber drives a Mercedes." Discussing inflation and crime during his town hall-style debate with Bottoms, he suggested Atlantans felt unsafe "at the gas store" during her tenure. When a citizen in the debate audience asked Jackson about minimum wage and affording basic necessities, Jackson told her, "Hopefully, you're not the one that is getting the $7.50 an hour."

Minimum wage is $7.25. Bottoms has proposed doubling it. Jackson has not proposed any increase. "My focus is creating jobs," he said. "I've been creating jobs my entire life."

Jackson's balancing act is enough for Debbie Satterfield, a 72-year-old who came to a Jackson rally in White County wearing both a Trump shirt and a Jackson sticker.

"When I heard about his harsh upbringing, and to hear how far he had climbed, and starting from nothing," she said. "It reminds me of my life starting with nothing. You can see his soul."

data.title: DOJ charges government contractor with leaking secrets to journalist girlfriend
data.description:
US accuses government contractor of leaking classified info to girlfriend's Substack

By Daniel Trotta
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 4:49 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Daniel Trotta

Oct 23 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department accused a government contractor on Friday of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, the publisher of a Substack newsletter.

The FBI arrested Ian Brinksman, ‌42, on Friday following a search of his Washington home, a Justice Department statement said. Prosecutors charged ‌him with unlawfully transmitting national defense information.

Advertisement

A federal public defender representing Brinksman declined to comment.

"As alleged, Brinksman reached far outside his own duties ​to obtain some of our Nation's most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them," John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said in the statement.

"That is not carelessness. It is a betrayal of his oath and the American people who entrusted him to fulfill his duties honorably," Eisenberg ‌said.

Brinksman held a top secret security clearance ⁠while working as an employee of a US government agency and later as a developer for systems integration for a private contractor working for the same agency, prosecutors said.

According ⁠to the sworn affidavit of an FBI agent investigating the case, Brinksman repeatedly accessed classified intelligence reports and then communicated with the journalist. The affidavit also cites phone records, database access logs, badge-swipe records, emails and other evidence.

The affidavit only ​identifies ​the journalist as "Individual 1," but it cites excerpts from articles ​she published.

"A fundraising article reportedly published by ‌Individual 1 in September 2026 stated 'over the past year (Individual 1 has) published reporting based on classified (relevant U.S. government agency) assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about,'" the affidavit reads.

That quote appears in a September 28 piece published on the Capital & Empire online newsletter authored by Aída Chávez.

"Over the past year, I've published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about," wrote Chávez, whose profile on the site ‌notes that she worked for the Nation and other outlets ​before she launched the newsletter.

Chávez did not respond to an email ​message seeking comment.

Investigators allege that on at least ​five occasions in 2026, Individual 1 published Substack articles containing information that mirrored the classified reports, ‌some at the top secret level. On some ​of those dates, Chávez published ​articles that cite classified reports, some of them attributed to the CIA.

According to a LinkedIn profile bearing Brinksman's name, he worked for Deloitte as a manager and as a senior strategy security consultant after having ​worked as a US State Department ‌foreign service officer on dates corresponding to those outlined in the Justice Department statement.

The State Department ​declined to comment. Deloitte did not respond to requests for comment.

(Reporting by Daniel Trotta in Carlsbad, ​California; Editing by Tom Hogue, Sergio Non, Rod Nickel)

data.title: Trump says noncitizen voting is a threat. A New York woman's arrest complicates the picture.
data.description:
New York state woman charged with voting illegally says she recently learned she wasn’t a citizen

PHILIP MARCELO
Updated Fri, October 23, 2026 at 9:00 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

An upstate New York woman who says she only recently learned she wasn't born in the U.S. has been charged with voting illegally, one of the latest arrests touted by the Trump administration as it hunts for noncitizen voters ahead of the midterm elections.

Marva Cook was adopted as a toddler and had always assumed she was a U.S. citizen, she told Homeland Security investigators earlier this month, according to the criminal complaint.

But in searching for her biological mother, the 66-year-old Syracuse resident, who starred on Syracuse University's women's basketball team decades ago, said she discovered she had a German birth certificate.

Advertisement

Federal prosecutors say Cook has had a green card for several years now, but she still cast ballots in recent elections despite not having citizenship.

She faces a single federal charge of voting by an alien stemming from her vote in the 2022 midterms.

The misdemeanor offense carries a maximum sentence of one year in prison and a fine up to $100,000, if convicted. Cook can also face deportation, under federal law.

Cook says she has faith in God and support from community

Reached by phone Friday, Cook declined to discuss the criminal case, her voting record or her past efforts at becoming a citizen.

But she said she was "not thrilled" by her court appearance Wednesday as she was placed in shackles despite having voluntarily turned herself in just hours earlier.

"It was a difficult time," Cook said. "I'm about kindness and service and doing for others as I want to be treated."

She also said she appreciated the outpouring of support of community members, a number of whom accompanied her to court Wednesday.

"The prayers and the support is a big part of how I will get through this," Cook said. "I have a deep faith that God will get me through it."

Cook's lawyer, Paul Tuck, also declined to discuss details of the criminal case Friday other than to say there are no upcoming hearings or filing deadlines. There are no pending immigration proceedings, he added, but Cook has an immigration lawyer in the event that changes.

Spokespersons for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement didn't immediately respond to emails seeking comment.

Cook is latest arrest in Trump's nationwide crackdown on noncitizen voting

First Assistant U.S. Attorney John A. Sarcone III, whose upstate New York office is prosecuting the case, said Cook's arrest showed "voter fraud is rampant" in the state.

Other federal agencies amplified the statement on social media, even as the administration's own investigations have demonstrated that such instances are incredibly rare and been shown not to change the outcome of elections.

"We cannot and will not allow the votes of American citizens to be canceled out by noncitizens illegally voting in our elections," the Homeland Security wrote in a post on X that included Sarcone's statement.

In California, federal authorities on Monday charged more than two dozen legal permanent residents with illegally casting ballots or registering to vote. Weeks earlier, 10 people were charged in Minnesota with illegally voting over the last three elections.

Supporters say Cook is a valuable member of the community

Cook's supporters, meanwhile, described her as a vital part of the local community where she had lived nearly all of her life and had starred in college basketball.

The Syracuse University athletics department confirmed Cook was the team's leading scorer in the 1979-80 season, averaging 15 points per game. She also holds the school record for most steals in a single season.

Fred Daley, pastor at All Saints Church, said Cook is an active member of the parish who for years has been the church's go-to Easter Bunny, decked out in full costume during the spring holiday season.

"If the government wanted to make a case, they chose the wrong person," he said. "She's a poster child of an amazing person. She's highly respected throughout the community."

Dale Avers, a parishioner who has known Cook for almost 20 years, described her as a "person of service" who "never sought limelight." She said Cook supports low-income families and youth as the YMCA's community school program director.

"I'm in total shock that they're putting this much effort into this," Avers said. "They understood the story. There was no intent. There's no malice. There was no deception involved."

data.title: Trump denies wanting a pool back in the White House but suggests he might move press
data.description:
POLITICS
Donald Trump

Trump suggests he might move press corps out of the White House

Mike Snider
USA TODAY
Oct. 24, 2026, 11:27 a.m. ET

President Donald Trump has suggested he may boot the journalists and media who cover the president from their longtime press briefing room inside the White House.

In a Truth Social post on Saturday, Trump said he "may move the Fake News to a less obnoxious location."

His comment comes after The New York Times reported Oct. 20 that Trump had told then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt in August to move reporters out of the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room, which has been the home of the White House press corps for more than five decades.

More: One key midterms race in all 50 states and why they matter

That idea wasn't put into action, and Leavitt departed later in the month. There's no current press secretary after the departure of Katie Zacharia, who held the job for five days earlier this month.

According to the Times, Trump also told aides that moving the press corps from its current position would allow for the return of an indoor therapy pool that was installed at the site during Franklin D. Roosevelt's administration. The Nixon administration replaced the pool with the press briefing room.

Midterm elections: Your guide to voting in the 2026 midterms? Here is what to know

Trump denied those plans in his social media post. "There is a Fake News report out there that I am going to remove the White House Press Room and bring back the old Swimming Pool, which lies directly underneath. Although I may move the Fake News to a less obnoxious location, the old swimming pool will never be brought back. I NEVER even thought to do such a stupid thing!"

Trump has regularly called out what he considers ​unfair reporting about his administration. In September, the president sought to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, saying he was frustrated by their reporting "fake news." A federal judge ordered the White House on Oct. 13 to continue allowing access to reporters from those outlets, although the Trump administration is contesting the ruling.

Prior to that, Trump banned the Associated Press in February 2025 when the outlet declined to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America in its coverage. A federal judge ordered the restrictions lifted in April 2025.

What is the White House Briefing Room?

Since 1970, the White House press corps has met in the press briefing room, which was constructed during President Richard Nixon's term. The small theater was designed especially for television news coverage.

The room was renamed the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room on Feb. 11, 2000, in honor of James Brady, the White House press secretary who was shot and seriously injured in an assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan on March 30, 1981. Reagan was also shot in the incident and spent a dozen days in the hospital recovering, according to the George W. Bush White House Archives.

A 2006 renovation led to improved work spaces, along with better online connections, lighting, and cooling; President George W. Bush reopen the renovated briefing room on July 11, 2007.

Contributing: Aysha Bagchi, USA TODAY; and Reuters.

Mike Snider is a national trending news reporter for USA TODAY. You can follow him on Threads, Bluesky, X and email him at  mikegsnider  &  @mikegsnider.bsky.social  &  @mikesnider & msnider@usatoday.com.

data.title: The U.S. has reportedly relied on Elon Musk to help shape foreign policy for years
data.description:
Exclusive-US has for years asked Musk to alter Starlink service in Ukraine, Middle East, sources say

By Erin Banco and Joey Roulette
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 12:51 AM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

FILE PHOTO: A Ukrainian serviceman of 47th brigade prepares a Starlink satellite internet systems at his positions at a front line the town of Avdiivka

1 of 4
FILE PHOTO: A Ukrainian serviceman of 47th brigade prepares a Starlink satellite internet systems at his positions at a front line, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, near the town of Avdiivka, recently captured by Russian troops in Donetsk region, Ukraine February 20, 2024. REUTERS/Inna Varenytsia/File Photo

By Erin Banco and Joey Roulette

WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Well before the throttling this month of Ukraine's military access to Elon Musk's satellite communications system, the Biden and Trump administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn its Starlink service on or off in various countries, according to six former senior US officials familiar with the matter.

During the presidency of Joe Biden, the requests included switching off the service to prevent Iranian proxy militias in Yemen and Lebanon from using Starlink to communicate, and ‌activating the service to provide internet access inside Iran and in Ukraine to support its military, said four of the former officials.

Advertisement

Similarly, President Donald Trump's administration asked Musk, who is CEO of SpaceX, to make the service available in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in ‌2025 and 2026, in hopes it would bolster internet access and communications for anti-government protesters, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters.

All of the people spoke on condition of anonymity. The previous US requests about Starlink access are being reported here for the first time.

The recent blowup over restrictions to Ukraine's use of SpaceX satellite services ​has raised questions about the ties between the US government and Musk, whose company owns systems vital to the US military and to US allies.

The Biden-era and Trump requests to Musk show a close relationship in which US administrations rely to an unprecedented degree on a private-sector company to help implement foreign policy.

The recent limits on Ukraine, despite being a US ally, have also rattled officials in Europe, some of whom argue that Europe must develop its own military satellite communications capabilities because no viable short-term alternative currently exists.

STARSHIELD RESTRICTIONS HOBBLE UKRAINE MILITARY

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last week that his country's access to Starshield, the military version of the Starlink system, had been intentionally limited, interfering with the performance of the country's military drones. He also said the speeds were reduced for Starlink, which Ukraine uses for some military activities including defense against Russian missile attacks.

Reuters has reported that the order to throttle Starshield came from inside the White House. The ‌Trump administration has acknowledged the slowdown but has not said whether it gave the order.

The White House, contacted ⁠for comment, referred Reuters to Trump's remarks on Friday, when he said he had not spoken with Musk about Starlink access issues for Ukraine and that "if there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out."

Halyna Yusypiuk, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said Ukraine's priority is "to have the service restored to normal speed as soon as possible, as the lives of our people depend on it."

SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment, although Musk said in ⁠a social media post earlier this week: "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately (by the president of the United States)."

Democratic US Representative Jason Crow called on Friday for clarity about the recent changes to Ukraine's satellite service, saying there are risks to the US dependence on SpaceX.

"Unelected billionaires and private corporations should not decide what is in the best interest of America's national security," Crow said.

For Ukraine, the Starlink internet service has become the lifeblood of frontline communication between units, who say there is currently no rival to the capabilities of SpaceX's products.

Starshield receivers, largely impervious to radio ​jamming, ​are used as onboard guidance systems and to provide links to a remote pilot for Ukrainian drones, including deep behind Russian lines inside Ukraine.

MUSK'S INFLUENCE RAISES UNCERTAINTY

Musk's role ​as the strong-willed CEO of a company with outsized influence over US national security has at times raised questions ‌over who is making decisions about SpaceX's satellite services.

The SpaceX CEO is "supposed to be a business executive, with government contracts, and he's essentially making huge foreign policy decisions," said Armand Musey, president of Summit Ridge Group, a satellite industry consultancy.

"He's sufficiently ambiguous of a person that you don't know if his decisions are sort of his personal quirks, or it's because there's an influence elsewhere that's impacting him," Musey said.

In previous years, Musk has moved to limit Ukraine's access to Starlink. In 2022, according to Reuters reporting, Musk ordered SpaceX personnel to cut Starlink coverage in areas Ukraine was trying to retake, a move that surprised White House officials.

Musk has said publicly that he refused a 2022 Ukrainian request to activate his satellite network in Crimea's port city of Sevastopol to aid an attack on Russia's fleet there, saying he feared complicity in a major act of war.

The Biden administration at times relied on Musk to help implement policy, five of the former officials said.

Biden officials coordinated with SpaceX to thwart US adversaries by cutting the service, and to help allies by expanding Starlink's availability, they said.

They added that discussions between the government and SpaceX, which usually included Pentagon and White House officials, often focused on ‌preventing groups such as the Iranian-linked Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon from using Starlink terminals.

Biden officials several times shared intelligence with SpaceX that indicated that the Houthis ​and Hezbollah were using diverted Starlink terminals — hardware that made its way to the militants through intermediaries.

In October 2023, during fighting between Israel and Hezbollah militants in southern Lebanon, intelligence ​officials told the White House that individuals linked to Hezbollah could have gained access to Starlink terminals. Officials had similar concerns about the ​Houthis in Yemen in 2024 during a US air campaign against the Iran-linked group, five of the officials said.

In both cases, the administration contacted SpaceX and asked it to identify the terminals and shut them off. At least some of ‌the terminals were deactivated, said two of the officials.

In a 2024 submission to the US Commerce Department's Bureau ​of Industry and Security, SpaceX said it works closely with US government agencies to ​secure export authorizations where required and to safeguard technology in support of US national security objectives and foreign policy goals.

Soon after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Biden officials pushed SpaceX to expand Starlink use for the Ukrainian military, said two of the former officials.

In a separate instance, the Biden administration asked SpaceX to turn on Starlink in Iran during a protest movement launched in September 2022 after the death of Mahsa Amini, an Iranian arrested for not wearing her hijab properly, according to one of the former officials.

Starlink terminals were ​moved into the country with the help of the administration, said the official, who declined to say how many ‌were transferred.

The Trump administration took a similar step earlier this year and discussed with Musk and SpaceX getting Starlink terminals into Iran and activated following US-Israeli strikes in the country in June 2025 and again in February 2026, a former senior Trump ​official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Neither the Trump administration nor SpaceX has publicly confirmed that those terminals were turned on. The Wall Street Journal reported in February that the US government had sent thousands of Starlink terminals into Iran.

Iran's ​delegation to the UN did not respond to a request for comment.

(Reporting by Erin Banco and Phil Stewart; Editing by Don Durfee and Edmund Klamann)

data.title: U.S. intelligence warns Iranian plots to kill Americans are in 'advanced stages'
data.description:
Politics

Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns

By
Olivia Gazis
Olivia Gazis covers intelligence and international security matters for CBS News. Twice Emmy-nominated, she has traveled worldwide with the secretary of state and contributes reporting on intelligence, foreign policy and other security topics across CBS News broadcast, radio, online and streaming platforms.
Read Full Bio
Olivia Gazis

October 23, 2026 / 11:13 PM EDT / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.

The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.

"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.

The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent. 

Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.

Axios was first to report on the memo.

The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.

"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."

A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.

Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people, including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.

Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks. 

Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.

"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

data.title: DOJ gives California counties 48 hours to help identify suspected noncitizen voters
data.description:
DOJ orders some California counties to verify ballots in 48 hours

SAFIYAH RIDDLE
Updated Sat, October 24, 2026 at 1:29 AM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Los Angeles (AP) — Federal prosecutors sent letters to county registrars across California on Friday demanding that local officials set aside and verify ballots that the Department of Justice said may belong to noncitizens, according to the Los Angeles County registrar and a letter obtained by The Associated Press.

The letters are the latest escalation in a legal battle between California and President Donald Trump's Department of Justice, which has recently focused on the state in its efforts to root out noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Data shows illegal voting by people who aren't U.S. citizens is incredibly rare, difficult to prove and has not been shown to change the outcome of races.

Earlier this month, the federal government targeted Los Angeles County and the California Secretary of State's office in a lawsuit that aimed to block them from counting the votes of roughly 20,000 people who are "likely" noncitizen voters. A hearing on the case is scheduled for Tuesday.

Advertisement

The Trump administration asked the 9th Circuit court of appeals to rule on the lawsuit barring a decision from the district judge assigned to the case. They set a deadline for Saturday.

Now, according to the LA County registrar's office, at least 18 counties across the state have received similar letters. They have been given a 48 hour deadline to provide identifying information corresponding with ballots that the federal government believes were sent to noncitizens illegally registered to vote. The letter requests that county officials also sequester any ballots where citizenship cannot be verified.

"Any election official who knowingly processes the ballot of a noncitizen is opening themselves to legal jeopardy," said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli.

The Justice Department is asking counties to send information about the voters it suspects are noncitizens including social security numbers, ID information, a copy of their registration and more.

That information can help the government and state quickly assess each person suspected of illegally registering to vote, said the letter sent to San Bernardino County voting officials. The letter says the government's list of suspected noncitizen voters includes 1,133 people from the inland Southern California county.

California's secretary of state and the Los Angeles County registrar have opposed the federal government's demands. In legal filings, lawyers for California say the request threatens to delay the certification of the vote and undermine the legitimacy of the November midterms. They have also argued that the federal government's data is unreliable and that their demands risk disenfranchisement of citizens.

Voting is underway in California, with the state's more than 23 million registered voters receiving ballots in the mail earlier this month. The state said in legal filings that over 330,000 mail-in ballots have already been counted.

The letters on Friday came on the heels of statewide sweep by federal authorities earlier in the week, where 28 people from the list of 20,000 were charged with illegally registering to vote. Some were also charged with illegally voting and lying on naturalization paperwork. Those charges could lead to years in prison.

data.title: Ukraine says Starlink restrictions remain despite Trump's claims they're lifted
data.description:
Ukraine says Starlink still restricted after Trump says limits lifted

5 hours ago
Hafsa Khaliland
Anastasiia Levchenko,Kyiv

Ukraine is still recording issues with the Starlink internet network, sources within the defence ministry say, after Donald Trump said limits had been reversed by Elon Musk who owns the satellite system.

The sources told the BBC that instances of drones experiencing connection loss at speeds of 161km/h (100mph) were being recorded, hampering military operations.

The US president had denied instructing the tech billionaire to restrict connectivity to Starlink's military-grade counterpart, Starshield, before saying on Thursday that Musk had "put it back".

Asked on Friday, Trump said: "If there is a problem, I will get it straightened out."

Trump added: "I have not spoken to him. I might have to, but I have not. I've heard it was fixed, but if it's not, I'll speak to him."

Musk previously said he was not behind the slowdown, which affected Ukraine's ability to use attack drones and co-ordinate defensive operations.

Trump told reporters he did not think the tech billionaire had too much power.

The Ukrainian defence ministry sources said the military was constantly monitoring the performance of both the Starlink and Starshield networks.

They added that there was "currently no confirmation that these restrictions have been lifted".

Last week, Kyiv said uplink speeds to the low Earth orbit satellites had been restricted, affecting the speed at which drones could travel. Any drone travelling faster than 100mph lost its connection, officials said.

Shortly after, Musk said that Starshield, which Ukraine uses for some of its operation, was controlled by the US military and suggested that the Pentagon could be behind the issues.

The White House has since repeatedly denied deliberately placing limits on the network in Ukraine.

In a call with Trump on Friday evening, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham "underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves against Russia's full-scale invasion", Downing Street said in a statement.

Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed.

The networks use 10,000 satellites to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and on the battlefield. Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.

Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

One Ukrainian soldier said there was "simply no alternative" to Starshield, adding that earlier in the week, connectivity had been cutting out when his unit had been travelling in a car at 80km/h (50 mph).

"I'll tell you this much: God forbid they shut it off completely - it would be an absolute catastrophe," he told the BBC. "We need a backup option for securing communications and internet."

Another soldier said they had reverted to the "proven algorithms" they used before they had Starlink when it initially started playing up, but stressed that Ukrainian forces did need the network, citing its speed.

"Even one or two seconds is critical when we can transfer data and orders faster," she said. "You can really feel that advantage on the battlefield."

Ukrainian reports of a slowdown to the service came during a tense diplomatic row between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky about Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.

Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.

While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.

Zelensky said the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump later denied.

The row prompted a war of words between the two world leaders, with Trump suggesting it was time for Ukraine to get a new president and Zelensky implying Trump was not a real leader.

Earlier on Thursday - before Trump's comments - Zelensky had said the speed of the system had still not been restored fully.

"I am waiting to hear from US Secretary of State [Marco] Rubio. He promised to get back to me with information within 48 hours or so."

The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had told Musk that he was frustrated the Starlink system's speeds were still capped, and that the system was working closer to normal following that conversation.
